A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same MiDl research, with matching authors, objectives, equations, and retained experiments. Text, tables, figures, and appendices are sufficiently readable for a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original recognition experiments on Epic-Sounds and Epic-Kitchens, including adaptation comparisons, Ego4D warm-up, and ablations in Tables 1–8.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Omnivore pretraining, mixed-modality streams, another loss ablation, qualitative cases, and direct Ego4D-AR evaluation.

M1.justification: The principal MiDl objective and online update procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B.5 introduces an evaluated variant applying KL distillation to individual modality predictions as well as audiovisual predictions; this is a limited loss extension, not a replacement of the main method.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates recognition directly on Ego4D-AR's diverse daily activities, whereas v1 uses Ego4D only for warm-up before kitchen-domain evaluation. Appendix B.4 also adds streams in which either audio or video can be missing, extending the earlier experiments that separately drop one designated modality.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds an unadapted Omnivore-pretrained baseline for comparison with its MiDl-adapted counterpart. SHOT, Tent, and ETA remain in the corresponding existing comparisons; Tent was already evaluated in v1 despite its incomplete enumeration in the accompanying prose.

E3.justification: Added settings include Omnivore initialization and equally divided audio/video omissions within mixed streams. Section 5.4 replaces the stated 25% Ego4D-AR warm-up selection with 5,000 training clips; whether these selections coincide is unspecified. Section 3.1 narrows missing-input filling from zeros or random data to zeros. The main online protocol and accuracy metric are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of pretraining sensitivity, mixed missing-modality robustness, and applying KL loss to every modality prediction (Tables 5, 9, and 10). Figures 3–4 additionally provide success and failure cases on both kitchen datasets. These substantially extend v1's architecture, component, and adapted-layer analyses.

E5.justification: v1 provides no explicit run counts, seeds, or variability estimates. v2 Appendix B.1 reports five runs with different seeds, and Table 11 supplies standard deviations for the main adaptation comparisons. This substantially improves uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Existing scores change: Table 1 reports MiDl's Epic-Kitchens accuracy at 75% missing video as 44.9% in v1 and 46.4% in v2. New results cover Omnivore, mixed streams, the KL variant, and Ego4D-AR; the latter reports 23.41% for MiDl versus 21.46% for the baseline at 75% missing audio. Qualitative outcomes are also added.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 explicitly assumes a nonzero probability of complete audiovisual samples for the intended stream, while retaining the zero-probability boundary evaluation. Section 5.3 adds corresponding long-stream reasoning. The principal objectives and Appendix A's mutual-information argument remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: framing missing modalities as online test-time adaptation and proposing modality invariance with self-distillation without retraining. Combining three contribution bullets into two preserves their substance, including the stated approximate 6% and 11% gains.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies validation as limited to audiovisual egocentric data and discusses adaptation-induced errors, including possible confusion from sinks and metallic objects. Section 6.4 also explains why MI-only adaptation can help at high missing rates despite harming complete-modality performance. These refine v1's broader interpretations without replacing the central explanation.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents official split proportions, grid-search selection of the unchanged loss weights, and use of one V100 GPU per experiment. It also replaces v1's code-link target, link.pdf, with a specific GitHub repository address. Repository contents or availability were not independently checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion or citations concerning dropout-induced modality bias, shared-specific feature modelling, auxiliary-task adaptation, real-time evaluation, and Omnivore pretraining. The fundamental positioning against training-dependent missing-modality methods and conventional test-time adaptation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, corrects the related-work heading, consolidates the contribution list, clarifies several method and evaluation paragraphs, and moves the author contribution statement to the end. The main section sequence and much of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The document receives a comprehensive ICLR-format layout change. Figures 1–2 are redrawn, with Figure 1 replacing a schematic trend with an Epic-Kitchens accuracy plot. v1 Tables 2–3 are merged, several tables are added or restructured, and two substantial qualitative figures are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad robustness claims relied mainly on two datasets sharing the same kitchen recordings and lacked reported uncertainty. v2 substantially strengthens their support through direct Ego4D evaluation, mixed-stream and pretraining tests, five-seed uncertainty reporting, and explicit failure cases and applicability limits. Reproducibility information also improves. Unexplained discrepancies remain: Table 8 retains the earlier 44.9% normalization-layer result while Table 1 reports 46.4%. This weakens the layer-ablation interpretation but does not outweigh the broader gains in validation and transparency.
